slides: Many counting questions have us choose from a pool. The pool can be digits, letters, books or people.

slides.say: And after every pick, we ask one question. Did the item leave the pool, or can we pick it again?

slides: That one question changes the count. Let's see how.

slides.say: Let's start with a tiny case. How many two-digit codes can we make from the digits one, two and three, if digits may repeat?
Here's the pool, one, two and three. For the first digit we have three options. Say we pick one.
Digits may repeat. So the one goes back into the pool, and we can pick it again.
Let's list every code. Eleven, twelve, thirteen.
Twenty-one, twenty-two, twenty-three.
Thirty-one, thirty-two, thirty-three. That's nine codes.
In stages, the first digit has three options, and the second digit has three options too, because the pool stayed full. Three times three is nine.
Now the same digits, but no digit may repeat.
The first digit again has three options. Say we pick one. This time the one leaves the pool. Only two digits are left.
Let's look at the same nine codes.
Eleven, twenty-two and thirty-three use a digit twice. They are not allowed now.
Nine minus three leaves six codes.
In stages, the first digit has three options, and the second digit only two. Three times two is six. The pool shrinks after every pick.
Now a bigger example. A code has three letters, from A, B, C, D, E and F. That's a pool of six letters.
If letters may repeat, every letter goes back to the pool. Each place has six options.
Six times six is thirty-six. Then thirty-six times six is two hundred sixteen codes.
If no letter may appear twice, the pool shrinks. The first place has six options.
at: If no letter may appear twice
The first place has six options

slides.say: One letter is used, so the second place has five. Two are used, so the third place has four.
Six times five is thirty. Then thirty times four is a hundred twenty codes.
The same letters, and a different answer. The only difference is whether a letter leaves the pool.
Putting different items in a row is choosing without repetition. Once an item is in its place, it's out of the pool.
Let's see it with three letters, A, B and C, in a row. Let's list every order.
at: three letters, A, B and C

slides.say: A first, then the other two in two orders. A B C, and A C B.
B first, B A C, and B C A. C first, C A B, and C B A. That's six orders.
Now in stages. The first place has three options. The second place has two, because one letter is already placed.
And the last place has only one letter left. No choice at all, so it gets one.
at: the last place has only one

slides.say: Three times two times one is six. The same six orders we listed.
at: Three times two times one is six

slides.say: Now a new example. Four different mugs stand in a row on a shelf. In how many orders can they stand?
The first place has four options, then three, then two, and the last place one.
Four times three is twelve. Times two, it's twenty-four. And times one, it's still twenty-four.
This product has a name. It's called a factorial, and we write it with an exclamation mark. Four times three times two times one is four factorial.
So n factorial is n, times every whole number below it, all the way down to one.
For example, three factorial is three times two times one, that's six.
Four factorial is four times three factorial. Four times six is twenty-four.
Five factorial is five times four factorial. Five times twenty-four is a hundred twenty.
So n different items in a row can stand in n factorial orders. We'll use factorial again later in this topic, when we choose groups.
at: n different items in a row

slides.say: So let's sum it up. After every pick, ask if the item can be picked again. If it can, the pool stays full.
at: If it can, the pool stays full

slides.say: If it left the pool, the pool shrinks by one at every stage.
And different items in a row are a choice without repetition. That's n factorial.

slides: Take a moment to memorize this, and I'll see you in the next video.
